en: Theravāda Vinayapiṭaka Cūḷavagga 15.
Khuddakavatthukkhandhaka (The Chapter on Minor Matters)
1. The Minor Matters.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, while bathing, were rubbing their bodies against trees—their thighs, their arms, their chests, and their backs.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, while bathing, rub their bodies against trees—their thighs, arms, chests, and backs—just like village wrestlers?
The monks heard those people criticizing, grumbling, and complaining.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, on this occasion and in this context, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the monks:
“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks, while bathing, rub their bodies against trees—their thighs, their arms, their chests, and their backs?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“Monks, it is unbecoming for those foolish men, it is unsuitable, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unallowable, and not to be done.”
"How indeed, monks, can those foolish men, while bathing, rub their bodies against trees—their thighs, their arms, their chests, and their backs?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
Having rebuked them..."
Having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, a bhikkhu who is bathing must not rub his body against a tree.
Whoever should so rub it commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, while bathing, the group-of-six monks rubbed their bodies against pillars—their thighs, their arms, their chests, and their backs.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, while bathing, rub their bodies against pillars—their thighs, their arms, their chests, and their backs—just like village wrestlers?"
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and expressing their indignation.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
"It is true, Blessed One"... [as before].
Having rebuked him … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, a monk who is bathing must not rub his body against a pillar.”
"Whoever should rub [his body] against a wall, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, while bathing, were rubbing their bodies against a wall—their thighs, arms, chests, and backs.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, while bathing, scrub their bodies against a wall—their thighs, arms, chests, and backs—just like village wrestlers?
… [After the inquiry] … “Monks, a monk who is bathing must not scrub his body against a wall.
Whoever should so scrub it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were bathing in improper places.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“…just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures.”
The bhikkhus heard those people grumbling, complaining, and carping.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… “Is it true, Blessed One? … “It is true, Blessed One. …
Having rebuked them … and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, one should not bathe in an improper place.”
"Whoever should bathe [in this manner], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks bathed using a "gandhabba-hand" (a scrubber).
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about... [as before]...
"Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
The bhikkhus heard those people criticizing, grumbling, and complaining about this.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before] ...
“Monks, one must not bathe using a fragrant powder.
Whoever should so bathe, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were bathing with *kuruvindaka* soap.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about, saying,
“… just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one must not bathe with *kuruvindaka* thread.
Whoever should bathe [with it], there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, having quarreled, had themselves perform services [for one another].
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
“…just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not have a preparatory bath performed by quarreling.
Whoever should have it performed, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were bathing with a scrubber.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying,
“…just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one must not bathe with soap powder.
Whoever should so bathe, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, a certain monk was afflicted by the disease of scabies.
He was not comfortable without a bowl-washer.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow an unglazed bowl-washer for one who is ill.”
Now at that time, a certain monk, being weak from old age, was unable to rub his body while bathing.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a back-scrubber,” he said.
Now at that time, the monks were hesitant to perform back-massages.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a broad-bristled brush,” he said.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks wore necklaces … they wore earrings … they wore neck-threads … [and so on].
They wear waist-bands …pe… they wear bracelets …pe… they wear armlets …pe…
They wear hand-ornaments ...
[and so on] ... they wear finger-rings.
People grumbled, complained, and became indignant ... [and so on].
"Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
The bhikkhus heard those people criticizing, disparaging, and complaining.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six monks wear strings of beads … pe … they wear anklets, they wear necklaces, they wear waist-bands, they wear bracelets, they wear hand-ornaments, and they wear finger-rings?
“It is true, Blessed One,” [they replied]. … pe …
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Bhikkhus, a creeper belt must not be worn …” [and so forth].
An ankle-ornament must not be worn… a neck-thread must not be worn… a waist-thread must not be worn.
An ankle-ornament must not be worn… a bracelet must not be worn… a hand-ornament must not be worn…
“Finger-rings must not be worn.
Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks wore long hair.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about,
saying, "They are just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, long hair must not be worn.
Whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow [hair] two months’ growth or two finger-breadths in length.”
Now at that time, the group of six monks were smoothing their hair with a brush...
they were smoothing their hair with a comb, smoothing their hair with a hand-comb, smoothing their hair with beeswax, and smoothing their hair with water-wax.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, hair should not be smoothed with a comb... [and so on]... ”
“Hair must not be smoothed with oil of sesame;
hair must not be smoothed with water-oil.
Whoever should smooth it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the group of six monks were looking at their own reflections in mirrors and in bowls of water.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
"They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not look at the reflection of one’s face in a mirror or in a bowl of water.
Whoever should look at it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Now at that time, a certain monk had a sore on his face.
He asked the monks,
"Friends, what kind of sore do I have?"
The bhikkhus said to him,
"Friend, such is your wound.
He did not believe them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, because of an illness, to look at the reflection of your face in a mirror or in a bowl of water.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks smeared their faces... [and so on].
They massage their faces, powder their faces, mark their faces with red arsenic, apply body ointments, apply face cosmetics, and apply both body ointments and face cosmetics.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
"These are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, the face must not be smeared with ointment...

the face must not be massaged, the face must not be powdered, the face must not be marked with red arsenic, no body-paint should be applied, no face-paint should be applied, and no body-paint or face-paint should be applied.”
"Whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, a certain monk suffered from an eye ailment.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to apply ointment to the face when there is a cause of illness.
Now at that time, there was a festival on the mountain slope in Rājagaha.
The group of six monks went to see the festival on the mountain slope.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying:
"How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, go to see dancing, singing, and instrumental music, just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not go to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music.
Whoever should go, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks sang the Dhamma in a drawn-out, melodic voice.
People complained, grumbled,
and became indignant, saying, “Just as we sing, so too do these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, sing the Dhamma with a drawn-out, melodic voice.
The bhikkhus heard those people complaining, grumbling, and becoming indignant.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks sing the Dhamma with a drawn-out, melodic voice?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Is it true, monks, that [this is so]?
… “It is true, Blessed One.
… Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Monks, there are these five disadvantages for one who sings the Dhamma in a drawn-out, melodic voice:

one becomes infatuated with that voice oneself, others become infatuated with that voice, householders grumble, concentration is broken for one who desires the art of vocal melody, and later generations follow one’s example.
These, monks, are the five disadvantages for one who sings the Dhamma in a drawn-out, melodic voice.”
“Monks, the Dhamma should not be sung with a drawn-out melodic voice.
Whoever should sing it so, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the monks were anxious about the recitation of the sacred word (sarabhañña).
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, the recitation of the scriptures (sara-bhañña),” he said.
Now at that time, the group of six monks wore wool with the fleece on the outside.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained, saying,
“They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, wool with the hair on the outside must not be worn.
Whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, mango trees were bearing fruit in the monastery of King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha.
King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha gave his permission, saying,
"Let the noble ones enjoy the mangoes as they please.
The group of six bhikkhus had young mangoes picked and ate them.
King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha had need of a mango.
Then King Seniya Bimbisāra of Māgadha gave orders to his men:
“Go, sirs, go to the monastery and bring back a mango.”
“Yes, Your Majesty,” those men replied to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha. They went to the monastery and said to the monastery guard, “Sir, the king needs mangoes;
give us some mangoes. “There are no mangoes, venerable sirs.”
“Having had the mangoes plucked while they were still quite young, the monks consumed them.
Then those people reported this matter to King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha:
“The masters have indeed made excellent use of the mangoes, sir; however, the Blessed One has praised moderation.”
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
"How can these ascetics, followers of the Sakyan, consume the king’s mangoes without knowing moderation?
The monks heard those people complaining, grumbling, and spreading it about.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, mangoes must not be consumed.
Whoever should consume them commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Now at that time, a certain group had provided a meal for the Saṅgha.
Amba seeds had been placed in the soup.
The bhikkhus, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept it... [as before] ...
“Accept it, monks; consume it.
I allow you, monks, mango seeds.
Now at that time, a certain association had prepared a meal for the Saṅgha.
They were unable to prepare mango pickles; instead, they gave whole mangoes right there in the dining hall.
The monks, being afraid of wrongdoing, did not accept them.
[The Buddha said: "Monks, accept them and consume them."
“I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to five ascetic concessions:

that which has been treated by fire, that which has been treated by a knife, that which has been treated by the fingernail, that which is seedless, and fifthly, that from which the seed has been removed.
I allow you, monks, to consume fruit according to these five ascetic concessions.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu had died after being bitten by a snake.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
"Surely, bhikkhus, that bhikkhu did not pervade these four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness."
For if, monks, that bhikkhu were to pervade these four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness, he would not die from being bitten by a snake.
What are the four royal families of snakes?
The Virūpakkha royal family of snakes, the Erāpatha royal family of snakes, the Chabyāputta royal family of snakes, and the Kaṇhāgotama royal family of snakes.
"Indeed, monks, that monk did not pervade these four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness.
For if, monks, that monk had pervaded these four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness, he would not have died from being bitten by a snake.
I allow you, monks, to pervade these four royal families of snakes with a mind of loving-kindness, for your own protection, for your own safety, and to perform a safeguard for yourselves."
And furthermore, monks, it should be done thus:
"May I have loving-kindness toward the Virūpakkhas;
may I have loving-kindness toward the Erāpathas."
I have loving-kindness for the Chabyāputtas,
and loving-kindness for the Kaṇhāgotamakas;
I have loving-kindness for those who are footless.
May there be loving-kindness for me from those with two feet;
may there be loving-kindness for me from those with four feet;
may there be loving-kindness for me from those with many feet.
May no footless creature harm me;
may no two-footed creature harm me;
may no four-footed creature harm me.
May no many-footed creature harm me.
May all beings, all living things,
and all creatures without exception—
May all behold auspicious things;
may nothing evil come to pass.
Boundless is the Buddha.
The Dharma is immeasurable;
the Saṅgha is immeasurable;
creeping reptiles are finite.
Against snakes, scorpions, centipedes,
spiders, crabs, and mice—
protection has been made for me, a safeguard has been established for me.
May the spirits depart!
I pay homage to the Blessed One;
I pay homage to the seven perfectly enlightened Buddhas.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, oppressed by lack of lust, cut off his own male organ.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, that foolish man has cut off one thing when he ought to have cut off something else."
“Monks, one’s own penis must not be cut off.
Whoever should cut it off commits a grave offense (thullaccaya).
Now at that time, a large ball of costly sandalwood appeared to a merchant of Rājagaha.
Then it occurred to the merchant of Rājagaha:
“What if I were to have this sandalwood block engraved?
The engraving will be for my own use, and I shall give the bowl as a gift.”

Then the merchant of Rājagaha had the bowl inscribed with that sandalwood block, hung it from a carrying-net, suspended it from the top of a bamboo pole, and having tied it to a succession of bamboo poles, he said:
"Whatever ascetic or brahmin is both an arahant and possessed of psychic power, let him take down this very bowl.
Then Pūraṇa Kassapa approached the merchant of Rājagaha, and having approached, he said this to the merchant of Rājagaha:
“I am indeed, householder, both an arahant and possessed of supernormal powers; give me your bowl.
“If, venerable sir, the venerable one is indeed both an arahant and possessed of supernormal powers, let him simply take away the bowl that has been given.
Then Makkhali Gosāla…
Ajita Kesakambala… Pakudha Kaccāyana… Sañjaya Belaṭṭhiputta…
The Nigaṇṭha Nātaputta approached the householder of Rājagaha, and having approached him, he said this to the householder of Rājagaha:
“Householder, I am indeed an arahant and possessed of supernormal power; give me your bowl.
“Venerable sir, if the venerable one is indeed an arahant and possessed of supernormal power, let him take away the bowl that has already been given.”
Now at that time, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna and the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja, having dressed in the morning and taken their bowls and robes, entered Rājagaha for alms.
Then the Venerable Piṇḍolabhāradvāja said this to the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna:
“The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is indeed an arahant and possesses supernormal power.”
“Go, friend Moggallāna, take down this bowl; this bowl belongs to you.
[Moggallāna replied:
“Venerable Bhāradvāja is indeed an arahant and possesses supernormal power.”
"Go, friend Bhāradvāja, take down this bowl; this bowl is yours.
Then the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja, having risen into the air, took that bowl and circumambulated Rājagaha three times.
Now at that time, the merchant of Rājagaha was staying in his own residence with his sons and wife, standing with palms joined in reverence, thinking:
"May the venerable Bhāradvāja establish himself right here in our residence, O Blessed One.
Then the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja established himself in the residence of the merchant of Rājagaha.
Then the merchant of Rājagaha took the bowl from the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja’s hand, filled it with highly valuable fresh food, and gave it back to the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja.
Then the Venerable Piṇḍola-Bhāradvāja took that bowl and went to the monastery.
People heard about this:
"It seems that the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja has discarded the bowl of the merchant of Rājagaha.
Those people followed closely behind the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, making a great clamor and a loud noise.
The Blessed One heard that great clamor and loud noise.
Having heard this, he addressed the Venerable Ānanda:
“Ānanda, what is this loud noise, this great clamor?
“Venerable sir, the bowl of the merchant of Rājagaha has been taken away by the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja.”
"Venerable sir, people heard that the bowl of the merchant of Rājagaha had been removed by the noble Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja.
And those people, venerable sir, followed closely behind the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja, making a great clamor and a loud noise."
“Thus, Bhante, it was this Blessed One who made such a loud noise and a great clamor.
Then, on that occasion and for that reason, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the Venerable Piṇḍola Bhāradvāja:
“Is it true, Bhāradvāja, that you removed the bowl of the guild-leader of Rājagaha?”
“It is true, Blessed One,” he replied.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked him:
“Bhāradvāja, this is unseemly, unsuitable, improper, unworthy of a recluse, unbecoming, and not to be done.”
"How is it, Bhāradvāja, that for the sake of a wretched wooden bowl you have displayed a superhuman feat of psychic power to householders?
Just as a woman might expose her private parts for the sake of a wretched copper coin, even so, Bhāradvāja,
have you displayed a superhuman feat of psychic power to householders for the sake of a wretched wooden bowl."
“Bhāradvāja, this does not inspire confidence in those without faith… Having rebuked him… and having given a teaching on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:”
“Monks, a superhuman state, a miracle of psychic power, must not be displayed to householders.
Whoever should display it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Break this wooden bowl, monks, by breaking it into pieces, and give it to the monks as a powder for applying collyrium.”
“Monks, a wooden bowl must not be used.
Whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks used various kinds of bowls, including those made of gold and silver.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about,
saying, “They are just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a bowl made of gold must not be used...
a bowl made of silver must not be used...
a bowl made of gemstone must not be used.”
A bowl made of beryl must not be used...
a bowl made of crystal must not be used...
a bowl made of bronze must not be used...
A bowl made of glass must not be used… a bowl made of tin must not be used… a bowl made of lead must not be used…
A bowl made of bronze or copper must not be used.
Whoever should use one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, two kinds of bowls: [those made of iron and those made of clay].
“An iron bowl, a clay bowl.
Now at that time, the base of the bowls was being scratched.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a bowl-stand.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks used various kinds of bowl-stands made of gold and silver.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just as with householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, you should not carry various high-quality almsbowls.”
Whoever should keep one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
“I allow you, monks, two kinds of bowl-bases:
one made of tin and one made of lead.”
The courtyards and the circular halls were not being swept.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to sweep,” he said.
They became frayed.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow you to cut [the hair] with a shark-tooth comb.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were carrying variegated bowl-rings, covered with painted figures like wall-paintings.
They wandered about showing them even on the carriage-roads.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, variegated bowl-rings, covered with figures and made as wall-paintings, should not be worn.”
Whoever should hold onto it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"I allow you, monks, a natural bowl-rim.
Now at that time, the monks were putting away their bowls while they still contained water.
A bowl with water stains becomes defiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, a bowl containing water should not be set aside."
"Whoever should put it away [while wet], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, to put the bowl away after it has been dried.
Now at that time, the monks were drying their bowls while they still contained water.
The bowl became foul-smelling.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a bowl containing water should not be left out to dry.”
"Whoever should heat it [with water], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, having made it free of water and having heated it, to put the bowl away.
Now at that time, the monks were storing their bowls in the heat.
The color of the bowl was spoiled.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, a bowl must not be kept in the heat.”
Whoever should set it on fire, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“I allow you, monks, after warming the bowl for a moment in the heat, to put it away.
Now at that time, many bowls were placed outside in the open air without support.
When they were turned over by a whirlwind, the bowls broke.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a bowl-rest,” he said.
Now at that time, the monks were setting down their bowls on the edge of the grass mat;
the bowls fell and broke.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, an almsbowl must not be placed on the edge of a terrace.
Whoever should place it there, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, monks were placing their almsbowls on the edge of a terrace.
Having fallen [on the ground], the bowl broke.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, a bowl must not be placed on a ledge."
"Whoever should set it down [on the ground], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the monks were setting their bowls face down on the bare ground;
the rim was being scratched.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a grass mat,” he said.
The grass mat was being eaten by termites.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a cloth-patch,” he said.
The cloth-patch was being eaten by termites.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a bowl-shelf,” he said.
But the bowl-shelf collapsed, and the bowl broke.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a bowl-rubbing board,” he said.
With the bowl-rubbing board, the bowl is polished.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a bowl bag,” he said.
But there was no shoulder strap.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a shoulder-strap and a binding cord,” he said.
Now at that time, monks were hanging their bowls on wall-crevices and on pegs.
Having fallen, the bowl broke.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, a bowl must not be hung up."
"Whoever should fasten it [to the bed], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Now at that time, monks placed their bowls on the bed; through forgetfulness, as they sat down, they covered them over and broke the bowls.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a bowl must not be placed on a bed.
Whoever should place it there incurs an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, monks placed their bowls on stools; through forgetfulness, they sat down and crushed the bowls, breaking them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, an almsbowl must not be placed on a bench.
Whoever should place it there, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the monks were placing their bowls on their laps; through forgetfulness, they would rise up, and the bowls, falling down, would break.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a bowl must not be placed on one’s lap.
Whoever should place it there, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the monks were placing their bowls under a sunshade.
In a whirlwind, the alms bowl was blown away and fell, breaking.

They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, for one who is ill, to carry a sunshade.
Now at that time, the monks thought:
“The Blessed One has allowed a sunshade only for one who is ill, not for one who is not ill.”
They felt guilty about carrying an umbrella in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to carry an umbrella in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery, even when not ill.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu, having hung his bowl from a carrying-sling and fastened it to his staff, passed through a certain village gate at an improper time.
People thought, "This is a thief going along; the flash of his sword is gleaming! They pursued him, seized him, and after recognizing him, released him.
Then that bhikkhu went to the monastery and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
"Friend, do you carry a staff?
"Yes, friend," he replied.
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires… [as before] … complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
“How can a bhikkhu wear a staff?
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One… [as before].
“It is true, Blessed One,” they replied.
… Having rebuked them … and having given a Dhamma talk, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks, a staff with a hook must not be carried.
Whoever should carry one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, a certain monk was ill and was unable to wander about without a staff.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to grant formal authorization for a staff to a sick monk.
And thus, monks, should it be granted:”

That sick monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his haunches and raised his joined palms, should speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, I am sick;
I am unable to wander about without a staff.”
‘Therefore, venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha for authorization to administer punishment.
It should be requested a second time;
it should be requested a third time.
A competent monk who is capable should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk named so-and-so is ill; he is unable to wander about without a staff.”
He requests formal authorization for punishment from the Saṅgha.
If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant formal authorization for punishment to the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This bhikkhu named so-and-so is ill; he is unable to wander about without a staff.
He requests from the Saṅgha authorization for a staff."
The Saṅgha grants formal authorization for the punishment of the monk named so-and-so.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of granting the formal authorization for the punishment of the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent;
whoever does not approve, let him speak.
“‘The authorization for the staff has been granted by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
Now at that time, a certain monk was ill and was unable to carry his bowl without a carrying-net.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to grant permission for a sick monk to carry his belongings in a sling.
And thus, monks, should it be granted:”

That sick monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the senior monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his hands in reverential salutation, should speak thus:
“Venerable sirs, I am sick;
I am unable to carry my bowl without a carrying-net.”
‘Therefore, Bhante, I request the Saṅgha for permission to carry [the bowl] in a sling.
It should be requested a second time;
it should be requested a third time.
A competent monk who is capable should inform the Saṅgha:
“Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This monk named so-and-so is ill; he is unable to carry his bowl without a carrying-sling.”
He requests the Sangha’s authorization for the carrying of a net.
If it seems appropriate to the Sangha, let the Sangha grant authorization for the carrying of a net to the monk named so-and-so.
This is the motion.
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me.
This bhikkhu named so-and-so is ill; he is unable to carry his bowl without a carrying-net.
He requests the Saṅgha’s authorization for a carrying-net."
The Sangha grants permission for the carrying of a carrying-net to the monk named so-and-so.
Whosoever among the venerable ones approves of granting permission for the carrying-net to the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent;
whosoever does not approve, let him speak.
“‘The Saṅgha has granted permission for the monk named so-and-so to carry a carrying-net.
It is pleasing to the Saṅgha; therefore, by silence, I hold this to be so.
Now at that time, a certain monk was ill; he was unable to wander about without a staff, nor was he able to carry his bowl without a carrying-net.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, I allow you to grant permission for a sick monk to carry a staff and a carrying-net.
And thus, monks, should it be granted:”

That sick monk, having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having bowed at the feet of the elder monks, having sat down on his haunches and extended his joined palms, should speak thus:

If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant permission for a staff and a carrying-net to this monk, named so-and-so.

The Sangha grants the authorization for the use of a staff and a carrying-pole to the monk named so-and-so.

Now at that time, a certain monk was a ruminator;
he would swallow after ruminating again and again.
The monks grumbled, complained, and became indignant:
“A monk is eating food at the wrong time.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, that monk has recently passed away from the womb of a cow.”
“I allow you, monks, for one who chews cud, the act of chewing cud.
But, monks, it must not be swallowed after having been brought out through the mouth-opening.
Whoever should swallow it is to be dealt with according to the rule.”
Now at that time, a certain guild had provided a meal for the Saṅgha.
In the dining hall, much rice was scattered about.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can it be that the recluses, sons of the Sakyan, do not receive the rice with due care when it is being given, [claiming] that ‘each single grain of rice is produced by a hundred acts of labor’?
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing.
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to take for yourselves and consume whatever falls while being given;
that, monks, has been relinquished by the donors.
Now at that time, a certain monk was walking for alms with long nails.
A certain woman, having seen that bhikkhu, said this to him:
"Come, venerable sir, engage in sexual intercourse.
"Enough, sister; this is not allowable," he replied.
“If you do not comply, venerable sir, I shall now scratch my limbs with my own fingernails and cause a disturbance, saying:
‘This monk has violated me!
“Understand this, sister,” he replied.
Then that woman, scratching her limbs with her own fingernails, made a scene,
saying, "This monk is violating me!
People ran up and seized that monk.
Those people saw both the skin and the blood on that woman’s nails. Having seen this, they thought:
“This deed belongs to this very woman; the monk is not the doer.”
They released that bhikkhu.
Then, having gone to the monastery, that bhikkhu reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
"But, friend, why do you wear long nails? they asked.
“Yes, friends,” they replied.
Then those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying, “How can a monk wear long nails?”
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, long nails must not be worn.
Whoever should wear them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).”
Now at that time, the bhikkhus were cutting their nails with their own nails, they were cutting their nails with their mouths, and they were rubbing them against walls.
Their fingers became painful.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow nail-clippers.
They cut their nails until they bled;
their fingers became painful. … [as before] …
“I allow you, monks, to trim the nails to the size of a grain of rice.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks had them trimmed smooth like a mirror.
People criticized, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just as if they were householders enjoying sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, a bedstead twenty-eight fingerbreadths [in height] must not be caused to be made.”
"Whoever should have [it] made, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, to scrape off only the surface dirt.
Now at that time, the hair of the monks had become long.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Bhikkhus, are you able to shave one another’s hair?
“We are able, Blessed One.”
Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having had the community of monks assembled...
[as before] ...addressed the monks:
"I allow you, monks, razors, razor-stones, razor-cases, nail-clippers, and all the equipment for shaving."
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks had their beards trimmed...
they had their beards grown long...
they had themselves shorn like a cow's tail...
They have them made square; they have them made with a border facing the front;
they have them made with a half-strip.
They have a beard grown;
they have hair removed from the private parts.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, you must not have your facial hair trimmed... [and so forth].”
One must not have the beard trimmed;
one must not have the hair on the body made like cow-hair;
one must not have it made square.
One should not have it made with a fringe;
one should not have it made as a half-dupatta;
one should not leave a tuft of hair.
"One must not have hair removed from the private parts.
Whoever should have it removed commits an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Now at that time, a certain monk had a sore on his private parts.
The medicine did not stay in place.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you, on account of illness, to have hair removed from the pubic region.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks had their hair cut with a razor.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying,
"They are just like householders who indulge in sensual pleasures."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, hair should not be caused to be cut with scissors.
Whoever should cause it to be cut, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, a certain monk had a sore on his head and was unable to have his hair cut with a razor.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One. [The Blessed One said:
“Monks, I allow you, on account of illness, to have the hair cut with scissors.”
Now at that time, the bhikkhus wore long nose-hairs.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about,
saying, "They are just like goblins."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, a long nose-hair must not be worn.
Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, monks were having nose-hairs extracted using pebbles and honey-dregs;
their noses became painful.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a comb.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks had their hair bleached.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about:
“It is just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not have oneself shaved with a razor.”
"Whoever should cause [it] to be taken, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the ears of a certain monk were blocked by earwax.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, an ear-cleaner.
Now at that time, the group of six monks used various kinds of ear-cleaners made of gold and silver.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, various types of ear-cleaners should not be carried.”
"Whoever should keep [such a vessel], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, [vessels] made of bone, ivory, horn, reed, bamboo, wood, lac, fruit, metal, and conch-shell.
Now at that time, the group of six monks accumulated a large quantity of metal ware and bronze ware.
People, while wandering on a tour of the monastery, saw this and complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, amass such a large collection of iron and bronze ware, just like bronze-vessel sellers?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not accumulate a large quantity of ironware or bronze ware.
Whoever should do so commits an offense of wrong-doing.
At that time, however, the monks felt guilty even over a collyrium box, a collyrium stick, an ear-cleaner, or even a mere binding cord.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, an eye-salve box, an eye-salve stick, an ear-wick for removing earwax, and a simple binding strap.
Now at that time, the group of six monks sat with their outer robes folded over their knees.
The alms bowls were being damaged by the outer robe.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
"Monks, one should not sit with the outer robe folded over the knees."
"Whoever should sit down [in such a manner], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was ill;
for him, it was not comfortable without a support.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, a yoke,” he said.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“How, then, should the weaving be done?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a shuttle, a loom, a frame, a weaver’s comb, and all weaving equipment.”
Now at that time, a certain monk who was not wearing a waistband entered a village for alms.
His inner robe slipped off on the street.
People raised a clamor.
Thus that bhikkhu was dejected.
Then that bhikkhu went to the monastery and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not enter a village without a waistband.
Whoever should enter [without one], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, a waistband.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks wore various kinds of waistbands—
a strap, a snake-skin band, a drum-shaped band, and a soft lute-shaped band.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“Just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, various kinds of waistbands should not be worn—”
The *kalābu* lute, the *deḍḍubhaka* lute, the *muraja* drum, and the soft *vīṇā* lute.
Whoever should carry these, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Monks, I allow two kinds of waistbands: [the *kaṭisuttaka* and the *veṭhana*].
“a strip of cloth, or a pig’s-ear [tassel].
When the fringes of the waistband wore out... [etc.
... “I allow you, monks, a muraja drum and a maddavīṇā lute.”
The inner lining of the waistband wore out … [as before] … “Monks,
I allow a beautiful woven band,” he said.
The outer edge of the waistband wore out … [as before] …
“I allow you, monks, a headband,” he said.
At that time, the group of six monks wore headbands of various kinds, including those made of gold and silver.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“Just as householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, you should not wear various kinds of elaborate dress.”
Whoever should wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
“I allow you, monks, [robes] made of bone …pe… made of conch-shell, made of thread,” he said.
Now at that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having put on light outer robes, entered a village for alms.
A whirlwind blew his outer robes away.
Then the Venerable Ānanda, having returned to the monastery, informed the bhikkhus of this matter.
The monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow, monks, a toggle and a cord,” he said.
Now at that time, the group of six monks wore toggles of various kinds, even those made of gold and silver.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about,
saying, "They are just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not wear a toggle of various kinds.
Whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Monks, I allow [a toggle] made of bone, ivory, horn, reed, bamboo, wood, lac, fruit, metal, conch-shell, or thread.”
Now at that time, the monks were attaching knots and loops to their robes,
and the robes wore out.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow a board with a cord and a board with a loop.
They attached both the board with a cord and the board with a loop to the edge [of the wall],
and the storehouse was opened.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to fix a wooden block for the cord at the edge;
you may fix a wooden block for the loop by inserting it seven or eight finger-breadths inside.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks wore laypeople’s garments:
those with an elephant-trunk design, those with a fish-scale pattern, those with four corners, those with a palm-leaf design, and those with a hundred stripes.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not wear the clothing of a householder.”
“An elephant trunk, a fish-scale pattern, a four-cornered pattern, a palm-leaf fan, and a hundred-fold fringe.
Whoever should wear [a robe with these patterns], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks wore the dress of householders.
People criticized, complained, and spread it about,
saying, “They are just like householders who enjoy sensual pleasures.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not wear the clothing of a householder.
Whoever should so wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks were wearing the *saṃvelliya* (a wrap-around garment).
People criticized, complained, and grumbled,
saying, "He is just like King Muṇḍavattī.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not wear a *saṃvelliya* (a wrapped garment).
Whoever should so wear it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Now at that time, the group of six monks carried a double-shoulder yoke.
People criticized, grumbled, and complained,
saying, "He is just like a king’s barber.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not carry a load on both shoulders.
Whoever should so carry it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, to carry a load on one shoulder, a load between [the legs], a head-load, a shoulder-load, a hip-load, or a suspended load.”
Now at that time, the bhikkhus did not chew tooth-sticks,
and their mouths became foul-smelling.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Bhikkhus, there are these five disadvantages of not chewing tooth-sticks:
the eyesight fails, the mouth becomes foul-smelling, the taste-buds are not purified, bile and phlegm coat the food, and the food does not agree with him.
These, bhikkhus, are the five disadvantages of not chewing tooth-sticks.”
“Monks, there are these five benefits from chewing a tooth-stick:
the eyes are clear, the mouth does not have a foul odor, the taste-buds are purified, bile and phlegm do not coat the food, and it cleanses the food one has eaten.
These, monks, are the five benefits from chewing a tooth-stick.”
“I allow you, monks, tooth-sticks.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks chewed long tooth-sticks and struck the novices with them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not chew a long tooth-stick.
Whoever should chew one, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Monks, I allow a tooth-stick no longer than eight finger-breadths, and a novice should not be made to clean it with it.”
"Whoever should strike [it], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, as a certain monk was chewing a tooth-stick that was too long, it became stuck in his throat.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not chew a tooth-stick that is too long.
Whoever should chew one, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
I allow you, monks, a tooth-stick no longer than four finger-breadths.”
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks were setting fire to a forest grove.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about,
saying, "They are just like forest-fire rangers!"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, a forest grove must not be set on fire.
Whoever should set one on fire commits an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, the monasteries were overgrown with thickets of grass; when forest fires broke out, the monasteries were consumed by the flames.
The bhikkhus were afraid to set a counter-fire or to perform a protective rite.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, when a forest fire is burning, to set a counter-fire and to perform a protective rite.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks climbed up trees and moved from tree to tree.
People complained, grumbled, and spread it about:
“It is just like monkeys,” they reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one must not climb a tree.”
"Whoever should mount [it], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, as a certain bhikkhu was traveling from the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī, an elephant attacked him on the way.
Then that bhikkhu, having run to the foot of a tree, did not mount the tree because he was filled with remorse.
Thus the elephant went away by another path.
Then that bhikkhu went to Sāvatthī and reported this matter to the bhikkhus.
The bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, when there is business to be done, to climb a man’s-height tree in times of distress as much as necessary.
Now at that time there were two brothers, monks named Yameḷa and Kekuṭa, born of brahmin stock, who were eloquent and possessed of beautiful speech.
They approached the Blessed One, and having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, they sat down to one side.
As they were sitting to one side, those bhikkhus said this to the Blessed One:
"At present, Bhante, there are bhikkhus of various names, various clans, various births, and various families who have gone forth.
They are corrupting the word of the Buddha with their own dialects."
"Come now, Bhante, let us set the word of the Buddha to verse.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
"How can you, foolish men, speak thus?"... [as before] ... "How indeed can you, foolish men, speak in such a way?"

“Come now, venerable sir, let us set the word of the Buddha to verse. “This will not lead to the confidence of those without faith, nor to the increase of the confidence of those who have faith,” he said, and having rebuked them... [as before]... he spoke in many ways in dispraise of their being difficult to correct. Then he addressed the monks: “Monks, this is an unfounded, baseless charge brought against me by those foolish men: ‘The Venerable Ānanda knows the Dhamma well; the Venerable Ānanda is a true disciple of the Teacher; it is from the Venerable Ānanda that we have heard and learned the Dhamma. Monks, whoever should say of me, ‘The Tathāgata taught the Dhamma for the sake of chanting,’ would speak what is contrary to fact and would be rebuked by the wise. For the Tathāgata did not teach the Dhamma for the sake of chanting. Whoever should say of me, ‘The Tathāgata taught the Dhamma for the sake of debate,’ would speak what is contrary to fact and would be rebuked by the wise. For the Tathāgata did not teach the Dhamma for the sake of debate. But rather, monks, the Tathāgata taught the Dhamma out of compassion for beings.
